Quezon Avenue, West Triangle, Quezon City www.dilq.qov.ph 8. 20u OPINIObel 30 Ms. CASEE GABUYA misscaseegabuya@qmail.com Dear Ms. Gabuya: This Department is in receipt of an electronic mail referral dated January 31, 2024, from COMELEC relative to your query on how to resign from your position as elected barangay official. At the outset, it may be well to note that resignation, as defined by the Supreme Court in Ortiz v. COMELECI, is the "act of giving up or the act of an officer by which he declines his office and renounces the further right to use it. It is an expression of the incumbent in some form, express or implied, of the intention to surrender, renounce, and relinquish the office and the acceptance by competent and lawful authority". Moreover, in the case of Sangguniang Bayan of San Andres, Catanduanes vs. Court of Appeals2, the Supreme Court held that to constitute a complete and operative resignation from public office, there must be: (a) an intention to relinquish a part of the term; (b) an act of relinquishment; and (c) an acceptance by the proper authority. The Local Government Code of 1991 (Republic Act 7160, hereinafter referred to as the Code) provides clear mechanisms on how to effect the resignation of local elective officials, such as sangguniang barangay members. In particular, Section 82 thereof provides: "Section 82. Resignation of Elective Local Officials. — (a) Resignations by elective local officials shall be deemed effective only upon acceptance by the following authorities: (I) The President, in the case of governors, vice-governors, and mayors and vice-mayors of highly urbanized cities and independent component cities; (2) The governor, in the case of municipal mayors, municipal vice-mayors, city mayors and city vice-mayors of component cities; (3) The sanggunian concerned, in the case of sanggunian members; and (4) The city or municipal mayor, in the case of barangay officials. 1162 SCRA 812 2 G.R. No. 11883, January 16, 1998 "Matino, Mahusay at Maasahan" Trunkline No.: 8876-34-54

(b) Copies of the resignation letters of elective local officials, together with the action taken by the aforesaid authorities, shall be furnished the Department of the Interior and Local Government. (c) The resignation shall be deemed accepted if not acted upon by the authority concerned within fifteen (15) days from receipt thereof. (d) Irrevocable resignations by sanggunian members shall be deemed accepted upon presentation before an open session of the sanggunian concerned and duly entered in its records: Provided, however, that this subsection does not apply to sanggunian members who are subject to recall elections or to cases where existing laws prescribed the manner of acting upon such resignations." (Emphasis ours) As could be clearly gathered from the afore-quoted provision, the resignation of a sangguniang barangay member is carried out by tendering resignation to the city or municipal mayor, as the case may be, and the subsequent acceptance thereof by the concerned authority. It is to be emphasized that a mere tender or offer of resignation is inefficacious. As expressly provided by law, the resignation shall only be valid and effective upon acceptance thereof by the city or municipal mayor, as the case may be. Accordingly, the validity and effectivity of such a resignation are contingent upon the acceptance thereof by the concerned authority—sans acceptance by the concerned authority renders such a resignation naught. To bolster this, the Supreme Court in Republic of the Philippines v. Singuin3 held that acceptance is necessary for the resignation of a public officer to be operative and effective. Without acceptance, resignation is nothing, and the officer remains in office. Resignation to be effective must be accepted by competent authority, either in terms or by something tantamount to an acceptance, such as the appointment of the successor. A public officer cannot abandon his office before his resignation is accepted; otherwise, the officer is subject to the penal provisions of Article 238 of the Revised Penal Code. The final or conclusive act of a resignation's acceptance is the notice of acceptance. The incumbent official would not be in a position to determine the acceptance of his resignation unless he had been duly notified therefor. This opinion is being rendered without prejudice to any contrary opinion of competent authorities or the courts. We hope to have guided you accordingly. Thank you.
